Vs.

full_judgment:
2. The petitioner filed Contempt Petition before this Division stating, inter alia, that an article under the caption "প্রধান বিচারপতি বেছে নেওয়া"- published in the Daily Prothom Alo dated 15th December, 2014 written by Mizanur Rahman Khan, a Journalist of the Daily Prothom Alo which has demeaned the qualification of the Hon'ble Judges of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh. The Article has not only demeaned but also questioned the ability and integrity of the Judges of this great institution. In his Article he has advocated for appointment of the highest seat of the Judiciary from the lower courts or outside as none of the present Judges of the Appellate Division are fit or qualified to be the Chief Justice as in one case integrity is in question and in other cases those are mediocre as those are expendable. It is pertinent to mention that the same columnist has been repeatedly maligning the judiciary for a number of years. Ultimately he was found guilty in Contempt Petition No. 7471 of 2014 by a Division Bench of the High Court Division and was given sentence till rising of the Court with a fine of Taka 5000 on his tendering unconditional apology on the day of delivery of judgment. The Editor of "The Daily Prothom Alo", Mr. Motiur Rahman has also tendered unconditional apology in that case and contended that the said contemptuous article was published without his knowledge. Thus, he was exonerated from the charges of contempt in that case. It is further stated that after reading the article the public perception with regard to the sitting Judges of the Appellate Division will be tarnished. The article is highly contemptuous and it will lower down the prestige and image of the Judges of the Appellate Division in the estimation of the public. 

 3. The contemner respondents in compliance with the above direction of the Court duly appeared in person before this Court on 5-1-2015 at 900 am and submitted written statement on their behalf stating, inter alia, that the Respondent No.1, Mr. Mizanur Rahman Khan, after completion of his studies started his career as a journalist. At present he is working with "The Prothom Alo" as Joint Editor. He has been associated with "The Prothom Alo" since October 2005. Previously he worked as the Deputy Editor at "The Daily Samakal" and Diplomatic Corresponding at "The Daily Jugantor," "The Daily Muktokontho" and "The Banglabazar." Earlier he also worked for "The Daily New Nation" and "The Weekly Dhaka Courier." He is a member of the National Press Club and the Dhaka Reporter's Unity. At the very beginning of his journalistic career he started taking keen interest in law and the Justice delivery system. Since then, for the last 20 years he has been researching and writing on the working of the Constitution, judicial independence, democracy, good governance, rule of law, separation of power, formation of a National Judicial Appointment Commission, and importance of greater financial autonomy for the Supreme Court and the financial benefits for the Judges giving comparative figures in other jurisdictions. He published his first book in March 1995 under the name “সংবিধান এবং তত্ত্বাবধায়ক সরকার বির্তক” which among other issues deals with judicial appointments and various constitutional issues. Since then he has numerous publications regarding those issues. The petitioner unearthed through his skilful investigation journalism the role of the foreign countries and international Community in our liberation war in 1971 and the brutal murder of our Father of the Nation in 1975. Besides those extensive researches, investigations and publications the Respondent No.1 submitted various key notes in various seminars, workshops, symposiums regarding Constitution, judicial independence, democracy, good governance, rule of law, and separation of power, Judicial administration of the Supreme Court both in and outside the country. The respondent No.1 was much attracted to the practice and jurisprudence developed by the learned Judges in different parts of the world, particularly in the Sub-Content including those contributed by Bangladesh Supreme Court. The source of respondents' learning and understanding of the full purport of constitutional mechanism regarding the appointment of Chief Justice derives from Article 95(1) read with Article 48(3) of the Constitution which is further expounded by various significant Judgments pronounced by the both Divisions of this Court in various cases. The Respondent No. 1 wrote various articles based on the principle laid down by this Court in those aforesaid landmark cases based on his understanding about those principles. The respondents No.1 while writing this article "প্রধান বিচারপতি বেছে নেওয়া" merely cited various views and opinions on this topic expressed by the eminent jurists of the Sub-Continent including those held by Mr. Justice Markandey Katju, a retired justice of the Supreme Court of India and Mr. Justice VR Krishna Iyer, an eminent retired Justice of the Supreme Court of India and a leading scholarly jurist of eminence whose opinion has been cited by the Supreme Court of Bangladesh in many cases: The writer also influenced by Arghya Sengupta, the former lecturer of law at Oxford University who did a PhD degree on the judicial appointment from Oxford University. The learned Advocate of this Court who filed the contempt petition regarding the article in question perhaps due to oversight did not realize that opinion expressed and the example cited in the article merely express the views of those authorities mostly as part of information sharing. It is stated that from the plain reading of the impugned Article it would appear that none of the opinions belongs to the writer of the Article. All are citations from various Articles written by celebrated jurists of India i.e "Choosing the Chief justice," written by Arghya Sengupta published in "The Hindu" dated 5 May, 2014; "Pick Chief Justice of India merit, and not seniority" by Justice Markandey Katju published in "The Times of India" dated 14 August 2014; "Some reflection on the choice of a Chief Justice" by Justice VR Krishna Iyer published in "The Hindu" dated May 11, 2014. In the past there has been no significant discussion regarding the appointment of the Chief Justice of Bangladesh. In the present scenario while various landmark judgments of the Supreme Court were delivered regarding this issue and at the same time aforesaid articles were written by the distinguished jurists of India on the self same issue respondent No.1 deemed it as part of his area of interest particularly when similar views have been echoed and reinforced in many of the discourses and the views reflected in several judgments of our Supreme Court. "The Daily Prothom Alo" being one of the largest Bengali dailies felt it is within its bonafide duty and legitimate role to write and share this information with the readers and public at large. The said publication by "The Prothom Alo" was never intended to tarnish the image of the court or any judge, nor to hurt or harm the efficacy of the justice delivery system. The said publication is bona-fide, reasonable and for public interest. 

 6. The contempt of Court is not defined anywhere with precision. Generally any conduct by which the course of Justice is perverted is called contempt. According to Oswald's Contempt of Court (3rd Ed.) page 1 "Contempt, in the legal acceptance of the term, primarily signifies disrespect to that which is entitled to legal regard; but as a wrong purely moral, or affecting an object not possessing a legal status, it has in the eyes of the law, no existence. In its origin, all legal contempt will be found to consist in an offence more or less direct against the Sovereign himself, as the fountain head of law and justice, or against his Palace, where justice was administered. This clearly appears from the old cases." 

 7. In the case of Rex vs Gray (1900) 2 QB 36 contempt of Court was defined as (1) Any act done or writing published, calculated to bring a court or a Judge of the Court into contempt or lower its authority, is contempt of court. 

 9. In James Evening post case (1742) 2 Atk. 469 at page 471 Lord Hardwicke, LC observed: "There are three different sorts of contempt. One kind of contempt is scantlings the court itself. There may be like wise a contempt of this court, or in abusing parties, who are concerned in causes here. There may be also a contempt of this court in prejudicing mankind against persons, before the cause is heard. His lordship further observed : "There cannot be anything of greater consequence than to keep the streams of justice clear and pure that parties may proceed with safety, both to themselves and their characters." 

 11. In the case of Ramnik Lal Nanadal vs State Pranhal Nan Chand AIR 1952 Kutch 74 it has been held that the contempt’s by newspaper should be more severally dealt with for the reason that damage to the dignity of a court is done more by publication in newspaper than in individual utterances. 

 12. In the case of Omesh Saigal vs RK Dalmia AIR 1969 Delhi 214 at page 218 it has been held that the purpose of contempt jurisdiction is to uphold the majesty and dignity of the law courts and the image of such majesty in the minds of public cannot be allowed to be distorted. 

 22. On a careful] reading of the article it is seen that the writer Mr. Mizanur Rahman Khan, a journalist of the Daily Prothom Alo wanted to demean the competence and qualifications of the learned Judges of the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court and he has questioned the ability and integrity of the Judges of the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court. Ignoring the norms he Advocated for the appointment of the highest sit of judiciary from the lower courts or outside as he has formed the opinion that none of the present Judges of the Appellate Division are competent and qualified to adorn the exalted office of the Chief Justice as "in the case of Senior most Judge integrity may be questionable" and "the honest person may be mediocre." Both of them are expendable. From the quoted passages it is abundantly clear that it tends to interfere with the administration of justice by scandalising the Judges and the Court. Moreover, the article contains innuendo, slanderous and contemptuous statements. 

 24. The Press sometimes wrongly assumes that they are privileged to say and publish anything with impunity. However, the Press has the same rights and liabilities as a common man. A journalist is entitled to comment generally on the incidents in the courts and these do not amount to contempt of court, but in a case that is pending, no one has a right to prejudice a case. 

 25. The law of contempt is not meant for protecting the Judges, but it is for the protection of the institution of judiciary from defamatory, libellous, vilificatory and unfounded attack and criticism. Parties to the litigation and the counsel are given some latitute in presentation of their cases or in presenting the recorded or oral versions of a document to the court, but they have to be careful not to transgres the line of decency or propriety to impute a bad faith to the Judge in an open court or outside the court. 

 26. In the instant case it appears that the comment made by the contemner respondents against the Judges of the Appellate Division in the offending article demeaning the position of the Judges of the Appellate Division and thereby questioned their competence and integrity which amounts to scandalizing the court and its Judges. It is the greatest type of contempt to scandalize the Judges or the court by publishing contemuous article in "The Daily Prothom Allo." In the facts and circumstances of the case, we find the contemner respondents guilty of committing contempt of court. 

 27. In the instant case contemner respondents have tendered unconditional apology and have thrown themselves at the mercy, of this court. In the Case of MB Sanghi vs High Court of Punjab and Haryana (1991) 3 SCC 600 the supreme court of India held that acceptance of apology is in the discretion of the Court which has to be exercised having regard to the circumstances of each case and that apology must be genuine and prompt and should not be an effort to get out of an inconvenient situation to escape punishment. In the case of MY Shareef vs Hon'ble Judges of the High Court of Nagpur reported in AIR 1955 SC 19 the Supreme Court of India observed as follows: 

 28. In the Case of Ramesh Chandra vs JR Chaudhury, 1996 CrLJ 1554 the counter-affidavit filed by the opposite party No. 2 he has mentioned that if Allahabad High Court comes to the conclusion that any contempt has been committed by him he tenders apology for the same. The High Court held that this cannot be a heartfelt apology. It merely a paper apology that to a conditional one and is by all means meaningless. In this context the observation made by the Supreme Court in the case of LD Jaikwal vs State of UP, 2 can be quoted advantageously: 

 "We do not think that merely because the appellant has tendered his apology we should set aside the sentence and allow him to go unpunished. Otherwise, all that a person wanting to intimidate a Judge by making the grossest imputations against him has to do is to go ahead and scandalise him, and later on tender a formal empty apology which costs him practically nothing. If such an apology were to be accepted as a rule, and not as an exception, we would in fact be virtually issuing a license to scandalize Courts and commit contempt of Court with impunity ------ We firmly believe that considerations regarding maintenance of the independence of the judiciary and the morale of the Judges demand that we do not allow the appellant to escape with impunity in the mere tendering of apology, which in any case does not wipe out the mischief." Therefore, apology must be sincere and unconditional. In the case of Shahidul Islam vs Mahbubul Alam, 51 DLR 485 a picture was deliberately depicted that as if the court stood in the way of the borrower's repayment of the loan. The High Court Division rightly found that in the news items the court had been maligned and scandalized to lower it in the estimation of the members of the public. The High Court Division formed the option that it was the great type of contempt to malign and scandalise the highest Court and its Judges by publishing untrue and twisted news and comments in the newspaper. Accordingly the condemners were found guilty of committing contempt of court. But considering the unconditional apology tendered by the condemners they were exonerated. 

 29. In instant case since the contemner-respondents offered unconditional apology for having committed Contempt of Court and left themselves to the mercy of the Court, we have accepted their unconditional apology with a caution to be careful in future while making comment on the qualifications, competency and integrity of the Judges of the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court or any other court of law.
